moduleTitle: Managing and analyzing test results in Tricentis Testim
learningObjectives: Describe how to debug tests during runtime by stopping, pausing, or stepping through them to identify issues efficiently.
Explain the process of organizing and filtering test results with result labels.
Articulate the process of tagging failed runs with failure types to capture valuable insights and improve test analysis.

elements.description: Rather than always running a test start to finish, Testim lets you Pause execution at any point, resume with Play, or run step-by-step to inspect state between actions. Breakpoints (manual, set by you, or virtual, created automatically when using step into/out/over or pause) mark exactly where execution should halt.

After a test pauses at a breakpoint, clicking the Play button ('Run Test') in the action menu resumes the test from that exact step — not from the beginning, and not skipping ahead. The breakpoint itself isn't removed just because execution passed through it.

You don't have to start from the very beginning to debug a later part of a test: hovering the arrow between two steps and clicking Play from here starts the run from the step right after that point — useful for quickly re-checking just the part of the test that's actually under investigation.

elements.text: This is the same debugging toolkit covered in more depth in the 'Debugging test cases' and 'Streamlining Testing and Debugging' modules — this course frames it specifically as part of the broader 'managing and analyzing results' workflow.

bulletPoints: Pause/Play, step-by-step execution, and manual/virtual breakpoints let you debug mid-run instead of only after the fact.
Clicking Run Test (Play) after a breakpoint resumes from that exact step — it doesn't restart, skip ahead, or remove the breakpoint.
Play from here (on the arrow between two steps) starts a run from a specific point, without repeating everything before it.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Organizing and filtering with Result labels

elements.description: Free-text labels attached to a run — distinct from the Labels applied to tests in the Test Library. Result labels are commonly used to record things like which application environment was tested, which application version was tested, or which user/system executed the run (examples: 'nightly-scheduler', 'v1.42.34', 'Jenkins', 'Staging').

elements.term: Adding and filtering by result labels
elements.description: Result labels are added as part of a Scheduler's Advanced Options when setting up a scheduled run. Once runs carry labels, both the Suite Runs / Test Runs pages and the Filter Remote Runs pane let you filter directly by a result label — alongside filtering by execution type (Execution, Label, Plan, Scheduler), branch, or browser.

bulletPoints: Result labels ≠ Test Library labels — they tag a RUN, not a test definition.
Common uses: environment, application version, or the user/system (Jenkins, a scheduler) that triggered the run.
Added via a Scheduler's Advanced Options; filterable on Suite Runs / Test Runs and in Reports.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Tagging failed runs with failure types

elements.description: A failed run can be tagged with a failure-type reason, turning a raw 'failed' status into a categorized one — the same kind of categorization used by the Failure Types report covered in test-results modules (e.g. Element not found, Element not visible, JavaScript Error).

Once failures are tagged, the failure-type filter can show only the runs tagged with a specific reason, and the Reports view's donut chart shows the percentage distribution of failure types (each tag's share of total runs, alongside its change vs. the previous period) — turning individual failures into a trend you can act on. Clicking a failure tag jumps straight to the Test Runs screen, pre-filtered to every run tagged with that type.

elements.text: What tagging does NOT do: it doesn't automatically fix the failing test, and it doesn't eliminate the need to manually log a defect in a bug tracker — it's a categorization and analysis aid, not an automated remediation.

bulletPoints: Tagging a failed run with a failure type turns it into filterable, reportable data.
Reports' donut chart shows the % distribution of failure types over a period, revealing trends.
Clicking a failure tag jumps to the Test Runs screen filtered to that type.
Tagging does NOT auto-fix tests or eliminate manual defect logging — it's an analysis aid.

examPitfalls.title: Assuming Run Test after a breakpoint restarts the whole test
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Expecting clicking Play/Run Test after a paused breakpoint to start the test over from step one.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Run Test resumes from the exact step where the test was paused — it doesn't restart, skip ahead, or clear the breakpoint that caused the pause.

examPitfalls.title: Confusing Result labels with Test Library labels
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Assuming a label applied to a run and a label applied to a test in the Test Library are the same mechanism.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Result labels tag a specific RUN (environment, version, triggering system); Test Library labels tag a TEST definition. They're filtered and used in different places.

examPitfalls.title: Treating failure-type tagging as an automated fix
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Assuming tagging a failed run somehow resolves the underlying issue or removes the need to file a bug.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Tagging is purely a categorization/analysis aid — it enables filtering and trend reporting, but the test still needs investigating and any real defect still needs to be logged manually.

practiceQuiz.scenario: What happens when the user clicks "Run Test" after reaching a breakpoint in Testim?

options.text: The test will skip to the next step.
The test will continue running from the breakpoint.

practiceQuiz.hint: It resumes exactly where it left off.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Clicking Play ('Run Test') resumes the test from the exact step where it was previously paused — it doesn't end the test, skip the next step, or remove the breakpoint.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Why would you use multiple result labels when executing tests in Testim?

options.text: To reduce the number of test cases executed.
To reduce the execution time for tests.
To ensure test results are archived correctly.
To track test execution across different environments.

practiceQuiz.hint: Think environment, version, and the system that triggered the run.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Result labels are commonly used to record things like which application environment or version was tested, or which user/system triggered the run — letting you track and filter execution across those different environments, not to reduce test count, execution time, or handle archiving.

practiceQuiz.scenario: What are the benefits of tagging test failures in Testim?

options.text: Ability to filter tests by failure type over a time period
Seeing the percentage of failures by type in reports
Eliminating the need to manually log defects

practiceQuiz.hint: It's an analysis/filtering aid, not an automated fix.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Tagging failures lets you filter runs by failure type over a selected period and see the percentage distribution of failure types in Reports — it does not automatically fix tests, and it doesn't remove the need to manually log real defects.

Tag a RUN (environment/version/trigger source) — added via Scheduler Advanced Options, filterable on Runs/Reports.
Categorizes a failed run — enables filtering by type and % distribution in Reports; not an auto-fix.
